title: AI Shopping Agents Handled Just 0.4% of Online Orders on Black Friday
yt_title: AI Robots Went Black Friday Shopping… and Made Just 0.4% of Orders
yt_description:
AI traffic to US shops more than doubled on Thanksgiving, but Bain says AI agents completed only 0.4% of online orders worldwide. Shoppers don't trust bots with their credit cards yet, Visa's test saw agents fail 42.8% of shopping tasks, and Amazon, eBay and about half of big retail sites block them.

script: Welcome to IT News, AI News! Black Friday is here, and the robots went shopping. Well... almost. On Thanksgiving, traffic from AI services to American shopping sites more than doubled compared with last year, according to Adobe. But consulting firm Bain says AI agents actually made just zero point four percent of online orders worldwide. By value, that is only zero point two percent. So the bots browse a lot, but they rarely pay. Why? Trust. In a Visa survey, fifty four percent of Americans used AI for shopping, but only twenty three percent trust it with payments. And there is a reason. Visa tested twenty two AI models on fifteen shopping tasks. They failed almost forty three percent of the time. Worse: in more than half of those failures, the agent still bought something. Surprise package, anyone? American Express found fifty two percent would let a bot buy groceries, but only fifteen percent would trust it with electronics. Then there are the stores. Amazon blocks outside shopping agents, and it is suing Perplexity over its Comet agent. eBay, United Airlines and Kohl's also restrict or block AI agents. Coach and Gap let them browse, but not check out. A test of two hundred big shopping sites found about half did not let agents like ChatGPT, Gemini or Meta's Muse shop at all. Even when the door is open, agents get stuck at login or payment. One Muse order for windscreen wipers was cancelled seventeen hours later. So who pays when a bot messes up? Best Buy says it is not responsible, while American Express promises to protect eligible customers. Still, the prize is huge. McKinsey thinks agent shopping could drive one trillion dollars of US activity by twenty thirty. So for now, humans are still holding the credit card. And the robots? They are fine with that. Mostly.
